  <div class="pp-overline">The Effect of Enhanced Border Enforcement on El Paso</div>
  <h1>Fences and Fortunes</h1>
  <div class="pp-sub">In 1993, El Paso got the border crackdown it asked for. We measure what it cost.</div>
  <div class="pp-byline">Robin Grier · Sam Absher · Kevin Grier</div>

  <div class="pp-stats">
    <div class="pp-stat">
      <div class="v">−$2,714</div>
      <div class="k">average household income, El Paso 2000, relative to control cities (−6%)</div>
    </div>
    <div class="pp-stat">
      <div class="v">−$23,194</div>
      <div class="k">average house value — roughly 23% below what it would have been</div>
    </div>
    <div class="pp-stat">
      <div class="v">≈ −$5.9B</div>
      <div class="k">cumulative net effect, 1994–2002, after crediting every crime reduction (2000 USD)</div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="pp-actions">
    <!-- TODO: replace # with SSRN / working paper URL and replication repo -->
    <a class="solid" href="#">Read the paper</a>
    <a class="ghost" href="#">Data &amp; code</a>
  </div>

<!-- ============================== 01 ============================== -->
<div class="pp-section">
  <div class="pp-secnum">01 · The Operation</div>
  <h2>A wall of agents</h2>
  <p>
    Before 1993, the Border Patrol mostly looked for unauthorized immigrants
    <em>after</em> they were already inside El Paso — a practice that amounted to
    stopping and searching people based on how they looked, and that ended in a
    federal class-action lawsuit. When the court granted relief, a new sector
    chief flipped the strategy: stop crossings from happening at all.
  </p>
  <p>
    On September 19, 1993, Operation Hold the Line put a visible line of agents
    along the border — over 400 of the sector's 650 agents, positioned within
    sight of each other, around the clock, backed by four helicopter patrols and
    a repaired nine-mile downtown fence. It worked on its own terms:
    apprehensions around El Paso fell 80–85% within weeks. Local approval
    topped 90%, and the operation became the template for border militarization
    in California and beyond.
  </p>

  <div class="pp-quotepair">
    <div class="pp-quote">
      “The rampant criminal problems in our downtown are gone.”
      <span class="attr">— Larry Francis, Mayor of El Paso, 1993</span>
    </div>
    <div class="pp-bigfact">
      <div class="v">~40%</div>
      <div class="k">estimated share of El Paso retail purchases made by Mexican
      consumers before the operation. The governor of Chihuahua answered the
      crackdown with a “Buy Mexican” campaign.</div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- ============================== 02 ============================== -->
<div class="pp-section">
  <div class="pp-secnum">02 · Two Cities, One Economy</div>
  <h2>The line ran through a single city</h2>
  <p>
    El Paso and Ciudad Juárez are not neighbors so much as halves. In the early
    1990s roughly 20% of all U.S.–Mexico overland trade moved through the area
    and over 150,000 people crossed the border every day — to work, shop, attend
    school, see a doctor. Juárez residents supplied labor to El Paso firms and
    an estimated 20–30% of the city's retail sales. Nearly two-thirds of El
    Pasoans spoke Spanish at home.
  </p>
  <p>
    Cutting crossings in a place like that is not a surgical strike on illegal
    entry. It reduces the supply of workers, the demand for goods, and the
    customer base of downtown businesses — all at once. Whether the net effect
    on El Paso was positive or negative is an empirical question. So we
    measured it.
  </p>
</div>

<!-- ============================== 03 ============================== -->
<div class="pp-section">
  <div class="pp-secnum">03 · The Measuring Stick</div>
  <h2>Compared to what?</h2>
  <p>
    You can't rerun the 1990s without the operation, so we build the
    counterfactual two independent ways.
  </p>
  <p>
    <strong>Households.</strong> Using the 5% Census samples from IPUMS —
    70,272 household records — we compare El Paso before (1990) and after
    (2000) the operation against three southwestern control cities: Tucson,
    Albuquerque, and Laredo, in a difference-in-differences design reweighted
    on age, sex, marital status, education, children, and Hispanic origin.
  </p>
  <p>
    <strong>The county.</strong> With annual county data we build a “synthetic
    El Paso” — a weighted blend of Pima (Tucson), Bernalillo (Albuquerque), and
    Webb (Laredo) counties, with weights chosen so the blend tracks real El
    Paso for the fifteen-plus years <em>before</em> 1993. If the blend matches
    El Paso's path up to the operation, its path afterward is a credible
    estimate of the El Paso that never got one. Annual data lets us verify the
    pre-treatment fit directly — and it is excellent.
  </p>
  <details class="pp-details">
    <summary>What exactly is in synthetic El Paso?</summary>
    <div class="body">
      <p>Each outcome gets its own recipe, matched on its own pre-1993 history:</p>
      <div class="pp-tablewrap">
      <table class="pp-table">
        <caption>Donor weights by outcome</caption>
        <tr><th>Outcome</th><th>Bernalillo, NM</th><th>Pima, AZ</th><th>Webb, TX</th></tr>
        <tr><td>Per-capita income</td><td>0.00</td><td>0.45</td><td>0.56</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Population</td><td>0.43</td><td>0.57</td><td>0.00</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Business establishments</td><td>0.77</td><td>0.00</td><td>0.23</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Property crime</td><td>0.06</td><td>0.75</td><td>0.19</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Violent crime</td><td>0.25</td><td>0.19</td><td>0.57</td></tr>
      </table>
      </div>
      <p style="font-size:0.88rem; color:var(--ink-mute);">
        Results are robust to expanding the donor pool to 15 border-region
        counties; see the paper's appendix.
      </p>
    </div>
  </details>
</div>

<!-- ============================== 04 ============================== -->
<div class="pp-section">
  <div class="pp-secnum">04 · Incomes and Homes</div>
  <h2>What households lost</h2>
  <p>
    By 2000, the average El Paso household earned <strong>$2,714 less</strong>
    than the control cities say it should have — a 6% drop, significant at the
    0.1% level. House values fell further: <strong>$23,194 below</strong> a
    counterfactual average of roughly $100,000. Since a house price capitalizes
    everything a location offers — jobs, amenities, safety — that 23% decline
    is a rough hedonic estimate of the operation's <em>net</em> effect on
    living in El Paso. Buyers who could price in the safer downtown priced in
    everything else too, and marked the city down.
  </p>
  <details class="pp-details">
    <summary>How do we know it isn't noise? The placebo test</summary>
    <div class="body">
      <p>
        Assign the “treatment” falsely to each control city and rerun the
        model. Nothing comes close to El Paso's decline:
      </p>
      <div class="pp-tablewrap">
      <table class="pp-table">
        <caption>In-space placebo “effects” (weighted DiD)</caption>
        <tr><th>Falsely treated</th><th>Income</th><th>House value</th></tr>
        <tr><td>El Paso (actual)</td><td class="neg">−2,714***</td><td class="neg">−23,194***</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Albuquerque</td><td>+480</td><td>+4,084**</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Tucson</td><td>+559</td><td>+2,395</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Laredo</td><td>+1,002</td><td>−5,776**</td></tr>
      </table>
      </div>
      <p style="font-size:0.88rem; color:var(--ink-mute);">
        Placebo income “effects” are small, positive, and insignificant. The
        only sizeable placebo on house values is a quarter the size of El
        Paso's, with mixed sign.
      </p>
    </div>
  </details>
</div>

    diverge and keep diverging; the number of businesses stalls; and property
    crime falls — the one promise the operation kept.

<!-- ============================== 06 ============================== -->
<div class="pp-section">
  <div class="pp-secnum">06 · The Bargain, Priced</div>
  <h2>Crime fell. It wasn't close to enough.</h2>
  <p>
    Crime reduction was the operation's selling point, so credit it in full:
    monetize every avoided property and violent crime using standard
    cost-of-crime values — generous ones. Then set those benefits against the
    income losses. The ledger is not close in any year:
  </p>
  <div class="pp-tablewrap">
  <table class="pp-table">
    <caption>Monetized net effect of Operation Hold the Line (millions of 2000 USD)</caption>
    <tr><th>Year</th><th>Income loss</th><th>Crime benefit</th><th>Net</th></tr>
    <tr><td>1994</td><td class="neg">−583.1</td><td class="pos">+5.8</td><td class="neg">−577.2</td></tr>
    <tr><td>1995</td><td class="neg">−411.9</td><td class="pos">+156.6</td><td class="neg">−255.2</td></tr>
    <tr><td>1996</td><td class="neg">−552.6</td><td class="pos">+65.5</td><td class="neg">−487.0</td></tr>
    <tr><td>1997</td><td class="neg">−447.4</td><td class="pos">+48.2</td><td class="neg">−399.1</td></tr>
    <tr><td>1998</td><td class="neg">−456.1</td><td class="pos">+50.9</td><td class="neg">−405.1</td></tr>
    <tr><td>1999</td><td class="neg">−528.2</td><td class="pos">+43.7</td><td class="neg">−484.4</td></tr>
    <tr><td>2000</td><td class="neg">−495.5</td><td class="pos">+82.9</td><td class="neg">−412.6</td></tr>
    <tr><td>2001</td><td class="neg">−1,692.7</td><td class="pos">+81.4</td><td class="neg">−1,611.3</td></tr>
    <tr><td>2002</td><td class="neg">−1,359.3</td><td class="pos">+72.2</td><td class="neg">−1,287.1</td></tr>
  </table>
  </div>
  <p class="pp-note">
    Crime benefit combines the property- and violent-crime columns of the
    paper's Table 5. Summing the net column: roughly −$5.9 billion over nine
    years, borne by a county of about 700,000 people. These figures count only
    income and crime — they exclude the operation's direct budget cost, which
    would push the net further down.
  </p>
  <p>
    The debate over border enforcement is usually a national one — about
    deportations, crime rates, and labor markets in the aggregate. What this
    ledger shows is a cost that debate mostly ignores: the bill handed to the
    border communities themselves.
  </p>
</div>

<!-- ============================== 07 ============================== -->
<div class="pp-section">
  <div class="pp-secnum">07 · Kick the Tires</div>
  <h2>For researchers (and skeptics)</h2>
  <p>
    The full batteries are in the paper; the short versions are here.
  </p>
  <details class="pp-details">
    <summary>Two designs, two datasets, one answer</summary>
    <div class="body">
      The household evidence (Census microdata, difference-in-differences) and
      the county evidence (annual aggregates, synthetic control) share no data
      and few assumptions. The DiD cannot show pre-trends; the synthetic
      control can, and its pre-1993 fit is excellent. Both find economically
      large, statistically significant losses.
    </div>
  </details>
  <details class="pp-details">
    <summary>Maybe El Paso was just different? The placebo tests</summary>
    <div class="body">
      Falsely treating Tucson, Albuquerque, or Laredo produces income
      “effects” of +$480 to +$1,002 — none significant, all the wrong sign for
      the skeptic's story. In the county analysis, El Paso's gaps exceed every
      constructible placebo in nearly all years.
    </div>
  </details>
  <details class="pp-details">
    <summary>Sensitive to the three-county donor pool?</summary>
    <div class="body">
      No. Expanding the pool to 15 counties leaves the pre-treatment fit
      excellent and the post-1993 income decline negative and significant,
      beginning right at the intervention.
    </div>
  </details>
  <details class="pp-details">
    <summary>Isn't the house-value decline double counting?</summary>
    <div class="body">
      We treat it as an alternative summary, not an addition. Because house
      prices capitalize local wages, amenities, and safety together, the ~23%
      relative decline is best read as a hedonic estimate of the operation's
      overall net effect — an independent check that lands in the same place
      as the income-based ledger.
    </div>
  </details>
</div>

<!-- ============================== 08 ============================== -->
<div class="pp-section">
  <div class="pp-secnum">08 · Materials</div>
  <h2>Paper, data, and code</h2>
  <p>
    Every number on this page comes from the working paper and its replication
    files. Household data are the public IPUMS 5% Census samples (1990, 2000);
    county data are from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Census Bureau's
    Business Dynamics Statistics, and the FBI's Uniform Crime Reports.
  </p>
